name: Chartreuse Green
lede: Chartreuse Green is a yellow-green named for the French liqueur, and for the Carthusian monastery that still makes it, recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1926.

sections.title: A liqueur's color
sections.body:
Our library dates Chartreuse Green to Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, with a first record of 1926 at plate 12, swatch L2 [1]. The word *chartreuse* names the yellow-green liqueur distilled by Carthusian monks, itself named for the Grande Chartreuse monastery; the color name modifies [[chartreuse]] with Green to mark it apart from chartreuse's pinker variants [1].

Our library's nearest everyday match is [[khaki]], 3.3 units of ΔE away, with [[sulphur-yellow]] and [[olive]] listed as close neighbors [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Chartreuse Green in only 140 of 23,781 paintings (0.59 percent), as photographed[2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 27 of 1,674 paintings, at three times the archive's overall rate [2]. It is over-represented in paintings from India (3.2 times expected) and the Kalighat school especially (11.9 times) [2]. Émile Bernard used it most relative to his own museums' baseline, in 4 of his 22 works here, 6.8 times expected [2]. It most often plays an accent inside a painting [2].
